A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided monoidal category with braiding $c$ and let
$X\in\mathcal C$. For every $n\ge2$ there is a canonical group homomorphism

$$\rho_n\colon B_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(X^{\otimes n})$$

characterized by the property that $\rho_n(\sigma_i)$ is the local braiding of
the $i$-th and $(i+1)$-st tensor factors: in a strict model
$\rho_n(\sigma_i)=1_X^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes c_{X,X}\otimes1_X^{\otimes(n-i-1)}$,
while in general $c_{X,X}$ is transported by the associativity isomorphisms and
the result is independent of those choices by braided coherence
([[thm-braided-coherence-via-underlying-braids]]). The actions are compatible
with the standard inclusions $\iota_n\colon B_n\to B_{n+1}$ for $n\ge1$:

$$\rho_{n+1}(\iota_n(\beta))=\rho_n(\beta)\otimes1_X .$$

For $n=0,1$, define $\rho_n$ to be the unique homomorphism from the
trivial group $B_n$ to $\operatorname{Aut}(X^{\otimes n})$, with
$X^{\otimes0}=\mathbf 1$. There are no local generators in these cases.
At $n=0$, let $\lambda_X:\mathbf 1\otimes X\to X$ be the left unitor. Compatibility means

$$\rho_1(\iota_0(e))=\lambda_X(\rho_0(e)\otimes1_X)\lambda_X^{-1}=1_X .$$

For $n=1$ the preceding compatibility formula is literal because both sides
are the identity of $X\otimes X$.

The statement holds for the braiding of [[def-braided-monoidal-category]] with
no choice principle.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-fusion-and-multifusion-category]]. A **dagger structure** assigns to every
morphism $f:X\to Y$ a morphism $f^\dagger:Y\to X$, conjugate-linearly, with
$(g\circ f)^\dagger=f^\dagger\circ g^\dagger$ and
$(f^\dagger)^\dagger=f$. A **unitary fusion category** is such a fusion
category equipped with this dagger so that every morphism space is a
finite-dimensional normed space, composition is submultiplicative,
$\|f^\dagger\|=\|f\|$, and $\|f^\dagger f\|=\|f\|^2$. Thus each
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(X)$ is a finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebra.
Positive endomorphisms are the elements of its usual $C^*$-positive cone
(equivalently $u^\dagger u$ for an endomorphism $u$); in particular, if $c$ is
simple and $\operatorname{End}(c)=\mathbb C\operatorname{id}_c$, then
$\lambda\operatorname{id}_c$ is positive exactly when $\lambda\ge0$. For any
morphism $f:X\to Y$, $f^\dagger f$ is positive in $\operatorname{End}(X)$;
also require $f^\dagger f=0$ to imply $f=0$. Semisimple direct-sum
decompositions can be chosen orthogonally:
their inclusions $i_j$ satisfy $i_j^\dagger i_k=0$ for $j\ne k$,
$i_j^\dagger i_j=\operatorname{id}$, and $\sum_j i_j i_j^\dagger=\operatorname{id}$.
Tensor product preserves daggers:
$(f\otimes g)^\dagger=f^\dagger\otimes g^\dagger$. Its associator and unit
constraints are **unitary**, meaning $\alpha^\dagger=\alpha^{-1}$,
$\lambda^\dagger=\lambda^{-1}$, and $\rho^\dagger=\rho^{-1}$.

The underlying fusion category is rigid, so its evaluation and coevaluation
morphisms satisfy the duality zig-zag identities. Those morphisms are not
required to be unitary isomorphisms. A braiding is additional structure; when
it is specified as a **unitary braiding**, each component satisfies
$c_{X,Y}^\dagger=c_{X,Y}^{-1}$. Positivity and unitarity are extra structure,
not consequences of the fusion rules or of the braid relations alone.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary fusion category and fix a set
$\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$ of representatives for the simple
isomorphism classes. Throughout this definition, the ordered input charges
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$, total charge $d$, and all internal edge charges are labels
in $\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$. Also fix a parenthesized binary fusion
tree. At each internal vertex with incoming charges $x,y$ and outgoing charge
$z$, choose one vector from an orthonormal basis of $V_{xy}^z$. An
**admissible labeling** assigns a representative charge to each internal edge
so that each chosen vertex basis is nonempty; a separate multiplicity-basis
index is retained at every vertex. Compose the vertex morphisms, inserting the
associators required by the chosen tree, to obtain a morphism from the
parenthesized input tensor to $d$. These composite morphisms are the
**fusion-tree vectors**. The family is called a **fusion-tree basis** when it
is an orthonormal basis of the fixed-input, fixed-total fusion space. For the
empty input list the tensor is $\mathbf1$ and its empty tree vector is
$\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf1}$ when $d=\mathbf1$; for one input $a_1$, the
only tree vector is $\operatorname{id}_{a_1}$ when $d=a_1$. The next local
lemma proves the basis property for every finite input list and includes the
dimension recursion ([[lem-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-dimension]]).

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary fusion category, let $\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$
be the representative set fixed in [[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]], and take
$a_1,\ldots,a_n,d\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$. Fix any parenthesized
binary tree $T$ on the ordered input list. The fusion-tree vectors of
[[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]] form an orthonormal basis of
$\operatorname{Hom}(T,d)$. Their number is

$$m_T(d)=\sum_{\substack{\ell\text{ admissible, with every internal label in }\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)}}\;\prod_{v\,\mathrm{internal}}N_{\ell(v_L)\,\ell(v_R)}^{\ell(v)},$$

where the leaves carry the inputs, the root carries $d$, and each internal edge
is labeled by a representative simple charge. For the left-associated tree on
$n$ inputs this gives $m_0(d)=1$ if $d=\mathbf1$ and $0$ otherwise,
$m_1(d)=1$ if $a_1=d$ and $0$ otherwise, and

$$m_n(d)=\sum_e m_{n-1}(e)N_{e a_n}^d\qquad(n\ge2).$$

Let $(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ be a monoidal
category ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **braiding** on $\mathcal C$ is a natural isomorphism

$$c_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\longrightarrow Y\otimes X$$

natural in both variables ([[def-natural-isomorphism]]) such that, for all
objects $X,Y,Z$,

$$\alpha_{Y,Z,X}\circ c_{X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}=(1_Y\otimes c_{X,Z})\circ\alpha_{Y,X,Z}\circ(c_{X,Y}\otimes1_Z),$$

and

$$\alpha_{Z,X,Y}^{-1}\circ c_{X\otimes Y,Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}^{-1}=(c_{X,Z}\otimes1_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,Z,Y}^{-1}\circ(1_X\otimes c_{Y,Z}).$$

These are the two **hexagon identities**. The invertibility of each
$c_{X,Y}$ is part of the data, not a consequence of the hexagons.

Every F-symbol matrix in orthonormal fusion-tree bases of a unitary fusion
category is unitary.

In a unitary braided fusion category, every R-symbol matrix in orthonormal
multiplicity bases is unitary.

Let $a,b,c,d$ be four simple input charges and $t$ a simple total charge. The
root associator identity

$$\alpha_{a,b,c\otimes d}\circ\alpha_{a\otimes b,c,d} =(\operatorname{id}_a\otimes\alpha_{b,c,d})\circ\alpha_{a,b\otimes c,d} \circ(\alpha_{a,b,c}\otimes\operatorname{id}_d)$$

has equal matrices along its two routes in the fusion-tree bases. If $A_1,A_2,A_3$
are the three successive matrices on the right and $A_4,A_5$ the two successive
matrices on the left, then

$$A_3A_2A_1=A_5A_4.$$

Each matrix coefficient sums over every intermediate simple charge and every
multiplicity-basis index.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary braided fusion category with associator $\alpha$ and
braiding $c$. For all objects $X,Y,Z$, its two hexagons are

$$\alpha_{Y,Z,X}\circ c_{X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z} =(\operatorname{id}_Y\otimes c_{X,Z})\circ\alpha_{Y,X,Z} \circ(c_{X,Y}\otimes\operatorname{id}_Z),$$

$$\alpha_{Z,X,Y}^{-1}\circ c_{X\otimes Y,Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}^{-1} =(c_{X,Z}\otimes\operatorname{id}_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,Z,Y}^{-1} \circ(\operatorname{id}_X\otimes c_{Y,Z}).$$

For simple input charges and a fixed simple total charge, the two route matrices
in each equation are equal in fusion-tree coordinates. Each entry is the sum
over all intermediate simple charges and multiplicity indices of the products
of the corresponding F- and R-block entries.

derivations.claim: By [F2], each generator matrix is a product of unitary operators: $T_i$ and $T_i^{-1}$ are unitary changes of orthonormal fusion-tree basis, and $R_i$ is unitary on every orthogonal pair-charge summand. Therefore $\rho_c(\sigma_i)^*\rho_c(\sigma_i)=I$ and every generator, as well as its inverse, is unitary.

By [F1], the local categorical braidings on the full tensor power satisfy the Artin relations and define a homomorphism for the fixed parenthesization. Finite semisimplicity and orthogonality in [F2] decompose that tensor power into total-charge blocks; naturality of the braiding makes each block invariant, so restriction to $V(x^n\to c)$ preserves the same relations. The pentagon and hexagon coordinate identities in [F2] identify those matrices with the same parenthesized composites; distant generators commute because they act on disjoint tensor factors. Hence the restricted assignment is a unitary representation of the Artin presentation.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ carry the subspace topology of
$\mathbb C$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]) and the multiplication of
$\mathbb C$, and let $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$,
$\varepsilon([t]):=\exp(2\pi i t)$, for the published one-dimensional torus
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).
Then $\mathbb T$ is a compact metrizable topological abelian group
([[def-topological-group]]), $\varepsilon$ is an isomorphism of topological
groups, and
$$|zw-z|=|w-1|,\qquad |z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$$
for all $z,w\in\mathbb T$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim:
The operator norm satisfies the triangle inequality: for every unit
vector $x$, $\|(S+T)x\|\le\|Sx\|+\|Tx\|\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$,
so taking the maximum gives $\|S+T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}+
\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Scalar homogeneity follows from [F2] and the same
maximum definition. Thus
$|\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}-\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}|\le\|S-T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ by applying
the triangle inequality twice. [F1, F2, algebra]

The formula is independent of representatives. If $A'=uA$ and $B'=vB$
with $|u|=|v|=1$, then
$\inf_{|z|=1}\|A'-zB'\|=\inf_{|z|=1}\|A-(u^{-1}zv)B\|$; as $z$ runs over the
unit circle, so does $u^{-1}zv$. [given, F1, algebra]

The map $z\mapsto\|A-zB\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is continuous: step 1.1 bounds
$|\|A-zB\|-\|A-wB\||\le\|(z-w)B\|=|z-w|\|B\|$. By [F3] and [F4] it attains
its minimum on the unit circle, so the infimum in the definition is a
minimum. Nonnegativity and symmetry follow from the norm axioms and the
substitution $z\mapsto\bar z$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

For classes $[A],[B],[C]$, choose minimizing phases $z,w$ for the pairs
$(A,B)$ and $(B,C)$ by [F3]–[F4]. The triangle inequality gives
$\|A-zwC\|\le\|A-zB\|+\|zB-zwC\|=d_P([A],[B])+d_P([B],[C])$, so taking the
minimum over phases for $(A,C)$ proves the triangle inequality. If
$d_P([A],[B])=0$, a minimizing phase satisfies $A=zB$, so $[A]=[B]$.
Conversely equal classes have distance zero. Therefore $d_P$ is a metric on
$PU(V)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

projector, $U\in U(\mathcal C)$ a logical target, and $W\in U(V)$ an ambient

$\widetilde U:=JUJ^*:V\to V$. Define the **logical block error** and
**leakage amplitude** by
$$\epsilon_{\mathrm{log}}(W,U):=\|PWP-\widetilde U\|_{\mathrm{op}}, \qquad \epsilon_{\mathrm{leak}}(W):=\|(I-P)WP\|_{\mathrm{op}}.$$
Both are finite operator norms. The first measures the compressed block
against the target; the second measures transfer from the code into its
orthogonal complement. They diagnose different errors.

In the ordered computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$ of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], define the identity and Pauli endomorphisms of $Q_2$ by
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The displayed sign in $Y$ fixes all later orientation and rotation conventions.

Work with actual unitary matrices, not equivalence classes modulo global phase. The $n$-qubit **Clifford normalizer** is

$$\mathcal C_n:=\{U\text{ unitary on }\mathcal H_n:U\mathcal P_nU^*=\mathcal P_n\}.$$

It is a group under matrix multiplication. Every scalar unitary $\lambda I$ with $|\lambda|=1$ belongs to $\mathcal C_n$ and has the same conjugation action as $I$; the chosen convention retains these distinct matrices.

Use simple labels $\mathbf1,\psi,\sigma$ with unit fusion and
$\sigma\otimes\sigma=\mathbf1\oplus\psi$,
$\sigma\otimes\psi=\psi\otimes\sigma=\sigma$, and
$\psi\otimes\psi=\mathbf1$. In the three-$\sigma$, total-$\sigma$ fusion
space, the intermediate-channel basis is $(\mathbf1,\psi)$. In the pullback
R convention of [[def-qc-tqc-r-symbol]], fix

$$F^{\sigma\sigma\sigma}_{\sigma} =2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad R^{\sigma\sigma}_{\mathbf1}=e^{-i\pi/8},\qquad R^{\sigma\sigma}_{\psi}=e^{3i\pi/8}.$$

These are sector data only. This item makes no claim about an all-label Ising
F/R table or global Ising ribbon coherence.

The phases above use the pullback convention in [[def-qc-tqc-r-symbol]]. In a
convention recording the eigenvalues of the object-level braiding itself, the
eigenvalues are the inverses of the displayed phases. This convention note
does not extend the sector data to any other Ising fusion space.

derivations.claim:
By [F3], $R_\psi/R_1=i$. Removing $R_1$ gives
$B_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$, and recoupling by $H=H^{-1}$ gives
$B_2=HB_1H$. Both are unitary because $H$ and $B_1$ are unitary. Put
$a=(1+i)/2$ and $b=(1-i)/2$, so $B_2=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}$.
Direct multiplication, using $a^2+ib^2=a$, $ab(1+i)=ib$, and
$b^2+ia^2=-a$, gives
$$B_1B_2B_1=\begin{pmatrix}a&ib\\ib&-a\end{pmatrix}
=B_2B_1B_2.$$
Thus these matrices define a unitary representation of the two-generator
Artin presentation of $B_3$, independently of any all-label Ising
coherence claim. [F3, algebra]

Direct multiplication gives
$B_1XB_1^*=Y$, $B_1YB_1^*=-X$, and $B_1ZB_1^*=Z$; also
$B_2XB_2^*=X$, $B_2YB_2^*=Z$, and $B_2ZB_2^*=-Y$. Thus each generator
conjugates every Pauli matrix to a signed Pauli matrix. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

Products and inverses of Pauli normalizers again normalize the Pauli
group: for normalizers $A,B$, $(AB)\mathcal P(AB)^*
=A(B\mathcal P B^*)A^*=\mathcal P$, and the inverse property follows by
conjugating the equality $A\mathcal P A^*=\mathcal P$ by $A^*$. The scalar
phase removed in step 1.1 has trivial conjugation action, so the physical
braids are projectively Clifford in this sector. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

In the ordered computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$ of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], define the identity and Pauli endomorphisms of $Q_2$ by
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The displayed sign in $Y$ fixes all later orientation and rotation conventions.

The displayed tensor powers are tensor maps on the ordered factors, using [[def-qc-tensor-map]].
Fix an integer $n\ge 1$. Let $\mathcal H_n=Q_2^{\otimes n}$ be the ordered tensor register of $n$ qubits from [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]], and let $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. We name the wires $1,\ldots,n$; wire $j$ is position $j-1$ in the source's $0$-based factor list. Bit tuples use the big-endian encoding from [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]], so the first wire is the most significant bit. Write $X_j$ and $Z_j$ for the tensor maps with the displayed one-qubit matrix on wire $j$ and the identity on every other wire. For $x,z\in\mathbb F_2^n$, set $X^x=\bigotimes_{j=1}^n X^{x_j}$ and $Z^z=\bigotimes_{j=1}^n Z^{z_j}$, where an exponent $0$ means the identity on that factor and an exponent $1$ means the displayed Pauli matrix. For $k\in\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$, define

$$P(k,x,z):=i^kX^xZ^z.$$

The **phase-aware $n$-qubit Pauli set** $\mathcal P_n$ is the set of these operators with matrix multiplication. Its scalar subset is $Z_n:=\{i^k I_{\mathcal H_n}:k\in\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z\}$. The product-and-adjoint theorem proves that $\mathcal P_n$ is a group and that $Z_n$ is its center.

Work with actual unitary matrices, not equivalence classes modulo global phase. The $n$-qubit **Clifford normalizer** is

$$\mathcal C_n:=\{U\text{ unitary on }\mathcal H_n:U\mathcal P_nU^*=\mathcal P_n\}.$$

It is a group under matrix multiplication. Every scalar unitary $\lambda I$ with $|\lambda|=1$ belongs to $\mathcal C_n$ and has the same conjugation action as $I$; the chosen convention retains these distinct matrices.

Let $V\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let
$U(V)$ be its unitary group. Two unitaries are **projectively equivalent**
when $A=zB$ for some $z\in\mathbb C$ with $|z|=1$; write $[A]\in PU(V)$ for
the equivalence class. Define
$$d_P([A],[B]):=\min_{|z|=1}\|A-zB\|_{\mathrm{op}}.$$
This is the distance after quotienting by one common scalar phase. The phase
is minimized over the unit circle; it is not chosen independently in
different charge blocks.

Let $m\ge2$ and let $\mathcal H=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m}$. A **Majorana
system of length $2m$** is a family of operators
$\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_{2m}\in\operatorname{End}(\mathcal H)$ satisfying
$$\gamma_j^*=\gamma_j,\qquad \gamma_j^2=I,\qquad \gamma_j\gamma_k=-\gamma_k\gamma_j\quad(j\ne k).$$
Its parity operator is $\Pi=i^m\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_{2m}$. For each adjacent
pair, put
$$Q_1(j)=\frac{I-i\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}}2,\qquad Q_\psi(j)=\frac{I+i\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}}2,\qquad U_j=\exp\!\left(-\frac\pi4\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}\right).$$

A **Majorana–Ising exchange interface** on a fixed parity sector consists of
such a system, a choice $\eta\in\{1,-1\}$ and the sector
$\mathcal H_\eta=\ker(\Pi-\eta I)$, together with the following explicit
model-identification hypotheses for every $1\le j<2m$: the Ising pair-charge
projections are identified with $Q_1(j),Q_\psi(j)$, and the exchange is
$R_1Q_1(j)+R_\psi Q_\psi(j)$ with the same relative phase
$R_\psi/R_1=i$. The last identity is required for all adjacent pairs as part
of the interface; the three-anyon supplier below establishes it only in its
stated sector and does not prove this all-$m$ identification.

derivations.claim: Reordering the $2m$ Majorana factors gives $(\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_{2m})^*=(-1)^m\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_{2m}$ and $(\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_{2m})^2=(-1)^mI$. Therefore $\Pi^*=\Pi$ and $\Pi^2=I$. Also $\Pi\gamma_j=-\gamma_j\Pi$ for each $j$, so $\gamma_1$ bijects the $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces; each has dimension $2^{m-1}$. Since each product $\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$ commutes with $\Pi$, every $U_j$, being a function of that product, preserves both parity sectors.

Put $A_j=i\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$. Then $A_j^*=A_j$ and $A_j^2=I$, so $Q_1=(I-A_j)/2$ and $Q_\psi=(I+A_j)/2$ are orthogonal complementary projections. The operator $U_j=2^{-1/2}(I-\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1})$ has eigenvalues $e^{-i\pi/4}$ on $Q_1$ and $e^{i\pi/4}$ on $Q_\psi$, whose ratio is $i$. By [F3], the channel exchange is therefore $(R_1e^{i\pi/4})U_j$; its common scalar has no effect on conjugation.

Let $c=s=2^{-1/2}$ and $A=\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$, so $U_j=cI-sA$ and $U_j^*=cI+sA$. Multiplication using $\gamma_jA=\gamma_{j+1}$, $A\gamma_j=-\gamma_{j+1}$, $\gamma_{j+1}A=-\gamma_j$, and $A\gamma_{j+1}=\gamma_j$ gives $U_j\gamma_jU_j^*=\gamma_{j+1}$ and $U_j\gamma_{j+1}U_j^*=-\gamma_j$. Every other $\gamma_k$ commutes with $A$, so $U_j\gamma_kU_j^*=\gamma_k$.

For $A=\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$ and $B=\gamma_{j+1}\gamma_{j+2}$, the Majorana relations give $A^2=B^2=-I$ and $AB=-BA$. Expanding with these identities gives $$U_jU_{j+1}U_j=-(A+B)/\sqrt2=U_{j+1}U_jU_{j+1}.$$ If $|j-k|\ge2$, then the two products $\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$ and $\gamma_k\gamma_{k+1}$ commute because moving their four distinct factors past each other contributes sign $(-1)^4=1$; hence $U_jU_k=U_kU_j$. Thus the $U_j$ satisfy the Artin braid relations. The common scalar in step 1.2 preserves these relations, since both sides of each relation have the same number of generators.

For $1\le k<m$ define the even Majorana monomials $\bar Z_k=i\gamma_{2k-1}\gamma_{2k}$ and $\bar X_k=\prod_{\ell=k}^{m-1}(i\gamma_{2\ell}\gamma_{2\ell+1})$. Each bilinear is a Hermitian involution; the bilinears in a fixed $\bar X_k$ have disjoint supports and commute, so every $\bar X_k$ is also a Hermitian involution. All these even monomials commute with $\Pi$ and preserve $\mathcal H_\eta$. Their supports show that the $\bar Z_j$ commute with one another, the $\bar X_k$ commute with one another, and $\bar Z_j$ anticommutes with $\bar X_k$ exactly when $j=k$ (their support intersection has odd size exactly in that case). The commuting involutions $\bar Z_1,\ldots,\bar Z_{m-1}$ have joint sign projections $\prod_k(I+\epsilon_k\bar Z_k)/2$ whose sum is identity, so at least one joint eigenspace is nonzero. Applying products of the $\bar X_k$ flips each sign independently; hence all $2^{m-1}$ joint sign eigenspaces are nonzero and orthogonal. Their number equals $\dim\mathcal H_\eta=2^{m-1}$ from step 1.1, so each is one-dimensional. In this basis the $\bar Z_k,\bar X_k$ are the standard logical Pauli generators. To see they exhaust the restrictions of all even Majorana monomials, label $\gamma_j$ by the $j$th standard vector of $\mathbb F_2^{2m}$. Even monomial labels form the $2m-1$ dimensional even-sum subspace, and the all-ones parity label lies in it. The labels of the $2m-2$ operators $\bar Z_k,\bar X_k$ are independent modulo the parity label: no combination uses coordinate $2m$, while the successive coordinates $1,2,3,4,\ldots,2m-1$ force in turn the coefficients of $\bar Z_1,\bar X_1,\bar Z_2,\bar X_2,\ldots,\bar Z_{m-1},\bar X_{m-1}$ to vanish. They therefore form a basis of the quotient of even labels by the parity label. Reordering and cancelling Majorana factors shows that monomials with the same label differ only by a scalar; on $\mathcal H_\eta$ the parity monomial is scalar. Thus every even Majorana monomial restricts to an element of the logical phase-aware Pauli group generated by the $\bar Z_k,\bar X_k$. By step 2.1 each braid sends every Majorana to a signed Majorana, so it maps this finite Pauli group into itself; invertibility and finiteness make the image equal to the group. Hence each exchange normalizes the logical Pauli group.

Conjugation gives a homomorphism from the projective Clifford group to the automorphism group of the phase-aware Pauli group. That Pauli group is finite, so its automorphism group is finite. The kernel consists of unitaries commuting with every logical Pauli; commuting with all logical $Z_k$ makes a unitary diagonal in the computational basis, and commuting with each logical $X_k$ forces every diagonal entry to agree. Thus the kernel is scalar and the projective Clifford group is finite. For $m\ge2$, $PU(2^{m-1})$ is an infinite Hausdorff metric space by [F2]: the classes of $\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{it},1,\ldots,1)$ are distinct as $t$ varies modulo $2\pi$. A finite subgroup is closed in a metric space, so this braid subgroup is not dense.

Take the skeletal complex-linear category whose simple labels are
$\mathbf1,\tau$ and whose objects are finite direct sums of them, including
the empty direct sum $0$. For objects
$A=\bigoplus_s s^{\oplus m_s}$ and $B=\bigoplus_s s^{\oplus n_s}$, set
$\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)=\bigoplus_s\operatorname{Mat}_{n_s\times m_s}(\mathbb C)$;
composition is block-matrix multiplication, dagger is conjugate transpose,
and the norm is the maximum of the operator norms of its blocks. Thus direct
sums are orthogonal. Define tensor product on simple labels by the fusion rules
$\mathbf1\otimes a=a\otimes\mathbf1=a$ and $\tau\otimes\tau=\mathbf1\oplus\tau$,
and extend it distributively to direct sums. For each allowed simple fusion
channel $c\subset a\otimes b$, let $i_{ab}^c:c\to a\otimes b$ be the
standard unit-vector isometric inclusion. Since the multiplicity space is
$V_{ab}^c=\operatorname{Hom}(a\otimes b,c)$, its orthonormal basis vector is
the adjoint projection $(i_{ab}^c)^\dagger:a\otimes b\to c$; retain
$i_{ab}^c$ itself for the coevaluation construction below. On simple-label
blocks, tensor a pair
of morphism matrices by their Kronecker product on multiplicity coordinates
and by the identity on each simple fusion channel; extend over direct sums.
This defines a bifunctor compatible with dagger. Use the strict unit gauge:
every F or R coordinate involving $\mathbf1$ is the identity. Put

$$\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad u=\phi^{-1},\qquad v=\phi^{-1/2}.$$

The only nontrivial associator blocks are

$$F^{\tau\tau\tau}_{\mathbf1}=[1],\qquad F^{\tau\tau\tau}_{\tau}=\begin{pmatrix}u&v\\v&-u\end{pmatrix},$$

in the intermediate-channel order $(\mathbf1,\tau)$. In the pullback R
convention of [[def-qc-tqc-r-symbol]], the exchange blocks are

$$R^{\tau\tau}_{\mathbf1}=x=e^{-4\pi i/5},\qquad R^{\tau\tau}_{\tau}=y=e^{3\pi i/5}.$$

Because these are pullback symbols, define the object-level braiding
$c_{\tau,\tau}$ on the $\mathbf1$ and $\tau$ summands by $x^{-1}$ and
$y^{-1}$, respectively. Every braiding with a unit input is the strict
identity. These fixed chiral data define the Fibonacci unitary braided fusion
category in this gauge; the verification checks every nontrivial pentagon and
hexagon sector.

derivations.claim:
Put $u=\phi^{-1}$ and $v=\phi^{-1/2}$. Since
$\phi^2=\phi+1$,
$u^2+u=1$ and $v^2=u$. Matrix multiplication then gives
$F^2=\begin{pmatrix}u^2+v^2&uv-uv\\uv-uv&u^2+v^2\end{pmatrix}=I$.
Both diagonal entries of $B_1$ have modulus one, so $B_1$ is unitary; $F$
is unitary because it is real and $F^*F=F^2=I$. The data in [F1] give
$r=R_\tau/R_1=e^{-3\pi i/5}$. Also $r^5=-1$ and
$r\ne-1$, so division of $r^5+1=0$ by $r+1$ gives
$r^4-r^3+r^2-r+1=0$. With $y=r+r^{-1}$, division by $r^2$ gives
$y^2-y-1=0$; since $y=2\cos(3\pi/5)<0$, it follows that $y=-u$ and
$r^2+ur+1=0$. Hence $B_2=FB_1F$ is unitary. [given, F1, algebra]

Write $B_2=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\q&t\end{pmatrix}$, where
$p=u^2+ur$, $q=uv(1-r)$, and $t=u+u^2r$. Then
$$B_1B_2B_1=
\begin{pmatrix}p&qr\\qr&r^2t\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B_2B_1B_2=
\begin{pmatrix}p^2+q^2r&q(p+rt)\\q(p+rt)&q^2+t^2r\end{pmatrix}.$$
The relations $r^2=-ur-1$ and $u^3=2u-1$ give $p+rt=r$; expanding the
remaining diagonal entries and using $u^2+u=1$, $v^2=u$, and
$r^2+ur+1=0$ gives $p^2+q^2r=p$ and $q^2+t^2r=-p$. Thus both matrices reduce to
$$\begin{pmatrix}u^2+ur&uvr(1-r)\\uvr(1-r)&-(u^2+ur)\end{pmatrix}.$$
The Artin relation follows entry by entry. [given, F1, algebra]

The off-diagonal entry of $B_1B_2-B_2B_1$ is
$q(1-r)=uv(1-r)^2\ne0$, because $u,v\ne0$ and $r\ne1$. Thus the generators
do not commute. They are not two copies of a single diagonal phase gate in
the same fusion basis. [given, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

If $\alpha\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$, then
$\{e^{2\pi i n\alpha}:n\in\mathbb Z\}$ is dense in the unit circle.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every subgroup $H$ of a finite-dimensional real
Lie group $G$ that is closed as a subset of $G$ has a unique smooth structure
making it an embedded Lie subgroup of $G$.

The countable-choice assumption is required by the currently available local

then

$$di_e:\operatorname{Lie}(H)=T_eH\longrightarrow\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$$

is injective and identifies $\operatorname{Lie}(H)$ with the Lie subalgebra
$di_e(T_eH)$ of $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Give $PU(2)$ the quotient metric from
[[def-qc-tqc-projective-gate-and-metric]]. The map
$$q:SU(2)\longrightarrow PU(2),\qquad q(A)=[A],$$
is a two-sheeted covering with kernel $\{I,-I\}$. It induces a topological
group isomorphism $SU(2)/\{\pm I\}\cong PU(2)\cong SO(3)$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Identifying $SU(2)$ with the unit quaternions,
conjugation on the imaginary quaternions defines a surjective two-sheeted
covering homomorphism

$$\rho:SU(2)\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad \rho(q)(v)=qvq^{-1},$$

whose kernel is $\{1,-1\}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Put $C=B_1B_2^{-1}$. Using $F^2=I$, $v^2=u$, and $r+r^{-1}=-u$, direct multiplication gives $\det C=1$ and $\operatorname{tr}C=r+r^{-1}+(2-r-r^{-1})u^2=u^2$; the last equality uses $u^2+u=1$, since $(2+u)u^2=1$. Thus the eigenvalues of the unitary $C$ are $e^{i\theta}$ and $e^{-i\theta}$, with $2\cos\theta=u^2=\phi^{-2}$.

The number $\phi^{-2}$ has minimal polynomial $x^2-3x+1$, whose other root is $\phi^2>2$. If $e^{i\theta}$ were a root of unity, then $e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}$ would have all algebraic conjugates of absolute value at most $2$, since every such conjugate is a sum of two roots of unity. The conjugate $\phi^2>2$ contradicts this. Hence $\theta/(2\pi)$ is irrational.

Let $\bar\rho:PU(2)\to SO(3)$ be the topological group isomorphism supplied by [F4], and transport the standard smooth Lie-group structure of $SO(3)$ to $PU(2)$ along $\bar\rho$. This transported structure has exactly the quotient-metric topology. The covering map $\rho:SU(2)\to SO(3)$ from [F6] satisfies $\rho=\bar\rho\circ q$ and is a smooth local diffeomorphism; hence $q=\bar\rho^{-1}\circ\rho$ is a smooth local diffeomorphism too, so $dq_I$ is an isomorphism on tangent spaces. Since $\theta/\pi$ is irrational by step 2.1, [F2] shows that the projective powers of $C$ are dense in the smooth circle $T=\{[\operatorname{diag}(e^{it},e^{-it})]:t\in\mathbb R\}\subset PU(2)$ after choosing an eigenbasis; under $\bar\rho$ this is the ordinary rotation circle about an axis. Thus $T\subseteq H$, the closure of the projective braid image, and $H$ is closed in the transported Lie group. By [A1] and [F3], $H$ is an embedded Lie subgroup. In the eigenbasis, $C-C^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(2i\sin\theta,-2i\sin\theta)$ is a nonzero tangent vector to the corresponding circle in $SU(2)$, so $dq_I(C-C^{-1})$ is a nonzero tangent to $T$ and lies in $\operatorname{Lie}(H)$.

Write $X=dq(C-C^{-1})\in\operatorname{Lie}(H)$. Conjugation by $[B_1]$ sends $T$ to a circle with tangent $\operatorname{Ad}_{[B_1]}X$. If these circles had the same axis, the rotation in $SO(3)$ induced by $[B_1]$ would either preserve or reverse that axis. A reversing rotation is a half-turn, but this projective generator has angle $3\pi/5\ne\pi$. If it preserved the oriented axis, it would commute projectively with $C$. Choose a determinant-one lift of $[B_1]$ to $SU(2)$, using [F4]. Its conjugate of $C$ would then be either $C$ or $-C$, because the kernel of $q$ is $\{\pm I\}$. The second case contradicts invariance of trace and $\operatorname{tr}C=\phi^{-2}\ne0$, so $B_1$ would commute with $C$, and hence with $B_2$, contrary to [F1]. Therefore the two axes are nonparallel. Under the standard identification of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ with $\mathbb R^3$, the Lie bracket is the cross product up to a nonzero scalar; the bracket of two nonparallel axes is nonzero and independent of both. Thus $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\mathfrak{so}(3)$ by [F3].

The identity component $H^0$ has the full dimension of connected $SO(3)$, so it is an open subgroup. A connected group has no proper open subgroup; therefore $H^0=SO(3)$ and $H=SO(3)$. By [F4], the projective braid image is dense in $PU(2)$. The only choice assumption is [A1], and the conclusion is projective; no efficient braid-length bound follows.

$\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$ of representatives for the simple
isomorphism classes. Throughout this definition, the ordered input charges
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$, total charge $d$, and all internal edge charges are labels
in $\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$. Also fix a parenthesized binary fusion
tree. At each internal vertex with incoming charges $x,y$ and outgoing charge
$z$, choose one vector from an orthonormal basis of $V_{xy}^z$. An
**admissible labeling** assigns a representative charge to each internal edge
so that each chosen vertex basis is nonempty; a separate multiplicity-basis
index is retained at every vertex. Compose the vertex morphisms, inserting the
associators required by the chosen tree, to obtain a morphism from the
parenthesized input tensor to $d$. These composite morphisms are the
**fusion-tree vectors**. The family is called a **fusion-tree basis** when it
is an orthonormal basis of the fixed-input, fixed-total fusion space. For the
empty input list the tensor is $\mathbf1$ and its empty tree vector is
$\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf1}$ when $d=\mathbf1$; for one input $a_1$, the
only tree vector is $\operatorname{id}_{a_1}$ when $d=a_1$. The next local
lemma proves the basis property for every finite input list and includes the
dimension recursion ([[lem-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-dimension]]).

be the representative set fixed in [[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]], and take
$a_1,\ldots,a_n,d\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$. Fix any parenthesized
binary tree $T$ on the ordered input list. The fusion-tree vectors of
[[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]] form an orthonormal basis of
$\operatorname{Hom}(T,d)$. Their number is

$$m_T(d)=\sum_{\substack{\ell\text{ admissible, with every internal label in }\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)}}\;\prod_{v\,\mathrm{internal}}N_{\ell(v_L)\,\ell(v_R)}^{\ell(v)},$$

where the leaves carry the inputs, the root carries $d$, and each internal edge
is labeled by a representative simple charge. For the left-associated tree on
$n$ inputs this gives $m_0(d)=1$ if $d=\mathbf1$ and $0$ otherwise,
$m_1(d)=1$ if $a_1=d$ and $0$ otherwise, and

$$m_n(d)=\sum_e m_{n-1}(e)N_{e a_n}^d\qquad(n\ge2).$$

Fix a unitary fusion category $\mathcal D$ and the representative set
$\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal D)$ of [[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]].
For an ordered list $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal D)$,
$n\ge1$, a total charge $c\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal D)$, and a
parenthesized input tensor $T$, let $V=\operatorname{Hom}(T,c)\ne0$,
equipped with that definition's orthonormal fusion-tree inner product.

$V=V(x^n\to c)$. Let
$\mathcal C=\mathbb C^k$ with its ordered orthonormal computational basis,
where $k\ge1$. A **fixed-charge encoding** is an isometry
$J:\mathcal C\to V$, so $J^*J=I_{\mathcal C}$. Its code subspace is
$J\mathcal C$, and its code projector is
$$P:=JJ^*:V\to V.$$
An encoding records a chosen subspace of a fusion space; it does not identify
that subspace with an object of the fusion category.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-fusion-and-multifusion-category]]. A **dagger structure** assigns to every
morphism $f:X\to Y$ a morphism $f^\dagger:Y\to X$, conjugate-linearly, with
$(g\circ f)^\dagger=f^\dagger\circ g^\dagger$ and
$(f^\dagger)^\dagger=f$. A **unitary fusion category** is such a fusion
category equipped with this dagger so that every morphism space is a
finite-dimensional normed space, composition is submultiplicative,
$\|f^\dagger\|=\|f\|$, and $\|f^\dagger f\|=\|f\|^2$. Thus each
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(X)$ is a finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebra.
Positive endomorphisms are the elements of its usual $C^*$-positive cone
(equivalently $u^\dagger u$ for an endomorphism $u$); in particular, if $c$ is
simple and $\operatorname{End}(c)=\mathbb C\operatorname{id}_c$, then
$\lambda\operatorname{id}_c$ is positive exactly when $\lambda\ge0$. For any
morphism $f:X\to Y$, $f^\dagger f$ is positive in $\operatorname{End}(X)$;
also require $f^\dagger f=0$ to imply $f=0$. Semisimple direct-sum
decompositions can be chosen orthogonally:
their inclusions $i_j$ satisfy $i_j^\dagger i_k=0$ for $j\ne k$,
$i_j^\dagger i_j=\operatorname{id}$, and $\sum_j i_j i_j^\dagger=\operatorname{id}$.
Tensor product preserves daggers:
$(f\otimes g)^\dagger=f^\dagger\otimes g^\dagger$. Its associator and unit
constraints are **unitary**, meaning $\alpha^\dagger=\alpha^{-1}$,
$\lambda^\dagger=\lambda^{-1}$, and $\rho^\dagger=\rho^{-1}$.

The underlying fusion category is rigid, so its evaluation and coevaluation
morphisms satisfy the duality zig-zag identities. Those morphisms are not
required to be unitary isomorphisms. A braiding is additional structure; when
it is specified as a **unitary braiding**, each component satisfies
$c_{X,Y}^\dagger=c_{X,Y}^{-1}$. Positivity and unitarity are extra structure,
not consequences of the fusion rules or of the braid relations alone.

Every F-symbol matrix in orthonormal fusion-tree bases of a unitary fusion
category is unitary.

Take the skeletal complex-linear category whose simple labels are
$\mathbf1,\tau$ and whose objects are finite direct sums of them, including
the empty direct sum $0$. For objects

$\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)=\bigoplus_s\operatorname{Mat}_{n_s\times m_s}(\mathbb C)$;
composition is block-matrix multiplication, dagger is conjugate transpose,
and the norm is the maximum of the operator norms of its blocks. Thus direct
sums are orthogonal. Define tensor product on simple labels by the fusion rules
$\mathbf1\otimes a=a\otimes\mathbf1=a$ and $\tau\otimes\tau=\mathbf1\oplus\tau$,

Let $J:\mathcal C\to V$ be a fixed-charge encoding, $P=JJ^*$ its code
projector, $U\in U(\mathcal C)$ a logical target, and $W\in U(V)$ an ambient
unitary. Its zero-on-the-complement target extension is
$\widetilde U:=JUJ^*:V\to V$. Define the **logical block error** and
**leakage amplitude** by
$$\epsilon_{\mathrm{log}}(W,U):=\|PWP-\widetilde U\|_{\mathrm{op}}, \qquad \epsilon_{\mathrm{leak}}(W):=\|(I-P)WP\|_{\mathrm{op}}.$$
Both are finite operator norms. The first measures the compressed block
against the target; the second measures transfer from the code into its
orthogonal complement. They diagnose different errors.

Let $V=P V\oplus(I-P)V$ be an orthogonal decomposition of a finite-dimensional
Hilbert space, let $U$ and $W$ be unitary operators on the two summands, and
let $T:=U\oplus W$. If an ambient unitary $G$ satisfies
$\|G-T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\delta$, then the logical block error of $G$ relative
to $U$ and its leakage amplitude both are at most $\delta$.

Let $V\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let
$U(V)$ be its unitary group. Two unitaries are **projectively equivalent**
when $A=zB$ for some $z\in\mathbb C$ with $|z|=1$; write $[A]\in PU(V)$ for
the equivalence class. Define
$$d_P([A],[B]):=\min_{|z|=1}\|A-zB\|_{\mathrm{op}}.$$
This is the distance after quotienting by one common scalar phase. The phase
is minimized over the unit circle; it is not chosen independently in
different charge blocks.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a Hausdorff topological space
([[def-hausdorff-space]], [[def-topological-space]]), with compact subsets as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **A point and a disjoint compact set are separated.** If $K \subseteq X$ is
   compact and $x \in X \setminus K$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$x \in U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
2. **Two disjoint compact sets are separated.** If $K, L \subseteq X$ are compact
   and $K \cap L = \varnothing$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$L \subseteq U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
3. **Compact implies closed.** Every compact subset of $X$ is closed in $X$.
4. **In a compact Hausdorff space the two classes coincide.** If in addition
   $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact, then a subset of $X$ is compact if and only if
   it is closed.

**The proof is written choice-free, and that is not a stylistic preference.** The
textbook argument says "for each $y \in K$ choose disjoint open $U_y, V_y$",
which is a selection over an arbitrary index set and therefore an appeal to the
full Axiom of Choice. What is done below instead is to take the family of **all**
open $V$ that admit some open $U \ni x$ disjoint from them — a family cut out by
a formula, with nothing selected — extract a finite subcover from it, and only
then make finitely many selections, which [[lem-finite-choice]] supplies as a
theorem of ZF.
